cards.title: Breaking two for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.area: Online algorithms
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid instance \(I\) of the scheduling problem defined below, \(A\) outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) within \(K(L(I)+2)^d\) bit steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\]
Here \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length. The same positive \(\varepsilon\), program and polynomial bound must work for every job count, machine count and remaining input parameter. The complete instance is supplied before scheduling begins. No unproved complexity assumption is included in this existence question.
cards.definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same fixed-factor approximation-existence question.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside the valid input domain. The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

Choose \(\varepsilon\), the program and its polynomial constants once, before all inputs. They cannot depend on machine count, job count, processing times or encoding precision. There is no additive slack or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; the empty instance is included.

For background notation, let \(\mathcal R\subseteq[1,\infty)\) be the set of universal multiplicative factors achievable by one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm per factor in this exact model, and put \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R\). The established factor-two algorithm makes this set nonempty. The current proposition is equivalent to \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}<2\), but does not require determining that infimum or attaining it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform deterministic algorithm with some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and the stated worst-case polynomial bit-time and feasibility guarantees, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation. Any positive constant improvement below factor two qualifies. A factor such as \(2-1/m\), whose improvement vanishes as the input machine count grows, does not qualify. Neither a guarantee for a fixed number of machines nor a restricted family of processing times settles the full target. A negative answer must exclude all positive constant improvements for all uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in this model. A conditional hardness result is only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. There is no minimum improvement of \(0.01\), and the task does not ask to determine the optimal ratio.
cards.why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.

importance.reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.

progress.text: Lenstra–Shmoys–Tardos establish the factor-two polynomial-time algorithm, a scheme for fixed machine count, and hardness for every ratio below \(3/2\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

Verschae–Wiese give a configuration-LP gap of two for unrelated graph balancing. The journal issue is dated August 2014; neither date is a later unrestricted algorithmic hardness result.
Bamas and coauthors prove the makespan-to-Santa-Claus reduction and the stated two-value special-case guarantees. The preprint record remains version 1.

context_blocks.text: The original source asks whether some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), independent of the instance, permits a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation. The 12 September numerical reformulation asked for the full optimal ratio. The user's 17 September choice restores the barrier question: any positive constant improvement suffices, including an improvement smaller than \(1/100\).

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
cards.definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.
cards.why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

importance.reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.

progress.text: Dobzinski–Dughmi distinguish universal truthfulness from truthfulness in expectation and separate their power in a restricted multi-unit setting.
Dobzinski proves exponential value-query requirements for universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation; arbitrary communication remains outside this lower bound.
Assadi–Singla obtain expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) approximation with universal truthfulness and polynomially many queries.
Assadi–Kesselheim–Singla improve the submodular and XOS factor to \(O((\log  \log  m)^{2})\); Theorem 2 uses at most n value and demand queries.
Christodoulou–Koutsoupias–Kovács–Vlachos establish constant truthful guarantees under graph eligibility restrictions, without solving unrestricted submodular auctions.

context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand answer can describe a preferred bundle in \(m\) bits even if finding it requires comparing exponentially many bundles. The price vector must also be sent and paid for in the communication bound. This explains why a communication-efficient mechanism can delegate difficult optimization to a bidder without being computationally efficient for that bidder. It also explains why a bound on the number of queries alone is not a complete bit-cost specification.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla’s FOCS 2019 result gives a universally truthful expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) welfare approximation with polynomially many queries. cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\), one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), and constants \(K>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), such that for every explicit nonnegative rational additive valuation matrix \(I=(v_{ij})\) of bit length \(L\), the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within \(K(L+1)^d\) steps and
\[\Pr\!\left[\min_{i\in[n]}\sum_{j:\,A(I)(j)=i}v_{ij}
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{C}\right]\ge\frac23?\]
The probability is over the algorithm’s internal fair random bits and concerns one allocation serving all agents simultaneously. The constants and program must work for every number of agents and items and every permitted valuation matrix. The optimum is the largest achievable minimum agent value under the same indivisibility constraints.
cards.definitions:
Instances and values. There are \(n\ge1\) agents, \(m\ge1\) indivisible items, and an explicit matrix \(v\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\). Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Agent \(i\) values any bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) by
\[v_i(S)=\sum_{j\in S}v_{ij},\qquad v_i(\varnothing)=0.\]
Entries are finite and may be zero; their magnitudes, denominators and ratios are unrestricted. An item can have different positive values for different agents. The input has no identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-degree, bounded-agent-count or bounded-number-of-values promise. Values are known centrally and are used in their given common units. Rescaling different agents’ rows separately generally changes the objective and the optimal allocation.

Encoding. For an integer \(z\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(z+1\) and let \(U(z)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where the last part has exactly \(\ell\) bits. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)\), followed in row-major order by \(U(p_{ij})U(q_{ij})\), where \(p_{ij}\ge0\), \(q_{ij}\ge1\) and \(v_{ij}=p_{ij}/q_{ij}\). Fractions need not be reduced. The total bit length of this encoding is \(L\); polynomial time includes reading these bits and performing arithmetic. This is an explicit matrix, not a value oracle or a succinct circuit.

Feasibility and objective. An allocation is a function \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), where zero means that the item is unallocated. Each item can belong to at most one agent and cannot be split. The bundle of agent \(i\) is \(S_i(a)=\{j:a(j)=i\}\), and
\[F_I(a)=\min_{i\in[n]}v_i(S_i(a)),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}F_I(a).\]
The maximum exists because there are finitely many allocations. It is a nonnegative rational number. Unallocated items are permitted; requiring all items to be assigned would leave the optimum unchanged because every value is nonnegative. No capacity limits, payments, incentives, entitlement weights or other constraints are imposed. The algorithm must output the actual assignment, encoded as \(U(a(1))\cdots U(a(m))\), rather than only an estimate of its value.

Algorithm and randomness. The computational model is a finite multitape Turing machine with independent unbiased random bits and no advice or oracle. A deterministic algorithm is allowed. A single polynomial bound must hold for every valid input and every random tape, including unsuccessful tapes. On every tape the output must be feasible. The program and its constants are fixed independently of \(n\), \(m\), \(L\) and the values; polynomial dependence on numeric values instead of their bit lengths does not qualify. Invalid encodings may be rejected. The probability in the formal statement concerns only the machine’s random bits, with the input fixed adversarially in advance.

Guarantee. The event \(F_I(A(I))\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/C\) says that every agent simultaneously receives at least that amount in the returned allocation. Separate expectation bounds for individual agents are different. There is no input distribution, additive loss, supplied optimum value or promise that the optimum is positive. On a zero-optimum instance any feasible allocation meets the multiplicative requirement, but the time bound still applies. The approximation constant can be arbitrarily large but finite and independent of all inputs; equivalently it can be an integer by rounding a real constant upward. No accuracy parameter is part of the input.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify a finite algorithm and a fixed constant \(C\), establish polynomial running time in the full binary input length on every random tape, establish feasibility on every tape, and prove the simultaneous \(2/3\)-probability guarantee for every valid matrix.

A negative answer must rule out every universal constant and every uniform randomized algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial bound. Ruling out only deterministic algorithms or one chosen constant, proving a gap for a particular relaxation, or exhibiting an instance defeating one method is insufficient. This is an unconditional proposition: hardness derived from a complexity assumption remains conditional unless that assumption is also established. In particular, a deterministic inapproximability statement under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) cannot silently be applied to randomized algorithms; a suitable randomized complexity assumption and reduction must be identified.

A factor growing with agents, items or bit length; a constant approximation in quasipolynomial time; a numerical estimate without an allocation; or an expectation guarantee for each agent separately does not meet the target. Neither do results restricted to identical values, restricted assignment, a bounded input parameter or different access to valuations.

context_blocks.text: The objective protects the least satisfied participant. Suppose two agents value each of two items at one. Allocating one item to each gives minimum value one, whereas giving both items to either agent gives minimum value zero. A lottery that gives both items to a uniformly chosen agent gives each agent expected value one, but its minimum value is always zero. This illustrates why the guarantee must concern the quality of one simultaneous allocation.

Even additive values allow substantial heterogeneity: an item can be extremely valuable to one agent, moderately valuable to another, and worthless to a third. Maximizing total welfare would assign each item to an agent valuing it most, independently of the other items. Maximizing minimum welfare couples those decisions because every agent needs adequate value from resources that cannot be reused. The valuations are inputs to the optimization problem, without strategic reporting constraints.

The name Santa Claus is used differently across papers. Some reserve it for restricted assignment, where each item j has a single intrinsic value \(w_{j}\) and \(v_{ij}\) is either \(w_{j}\) or zero. This card uses the broader max-min allocation problem with arbitrary entries. The difference is decisive: constant-factor algorithms are known for restricted assignment, while the general constant-factor question remains open.

Chakrabarty, Chuzhoy and Khanna obtain \(O(m^\varepsilon)\)-approximation in polynomial time for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), where \(m\) counts items here. Their more precise tradeoff includes logarithmic factors and has an exponent depending on \(1/\varepsilon\); it also gives a polylogarithmic approximation in quasipolynomial time. The result does not give a polynomial-time constant factor by making \(\varepsilon\) depend on the instance size.

The standard configuration relaxation can overestimate the integral optimum by an unbounded factor on general additive instances. For a target value \(T\), its variables fractionally select bundles worth at least \(T\) for each agent while limiting the total fractional use of each item. The gap means that a feasible fractional target need not correspond to a comparable actual allocation. This limitation of one relaxation is distinct from an impossibility theorem for all polynomial-time algorithms.

Haxell and Szabó’s published 2025 theorem bounds the restricted-assignment configuration-LP integrality gap by \(53/15\), reported as less than 3.534. This compares fractional and integral optima in that particular model. A good integral allocation’s existence is also different from a polynomial-time procedure constructing it. The theorem supplies neither a general additive approximation nor a matching impossibility result.

Bamas, Lindermayr, Megow, Rohwedder and Schlöter connect this question to unrelated-machine makespan. A polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for that scheduling problem, for fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields an \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation here for every fixed \(\delta>0\). Thus any fixed improvement below two in general unrelated makespan would give a constant allocation factor. Their general implication is one-way; the reverse equivalence in the paper has a two-value restriction.

The SODA 2025 submodular result extends the small-power polynomial-time and polylogarithmic quasipolynomial-time guarantees to monotone submodular preferences. Submodularity means diminishing marginal returns when a bundle grows. Those more general preferences are accessed through value queries, whereas the current card gives an explicit additive matrix. The improvement in preference scope leaves a growing factor on general additive instances.

Boehmer’s SWAT 2026 result guarantees at least \(2/5\) of optimum for identical monotone submodular valuations. In the approximation-factor convention used here this would be a factor \(5/2\), but only for that restricted input class. Allowing diminishing returns does not remove the separate assumption that every agent has the same preferences.

The distributed paper’s September 2026 revision gives each gift one intrinsic value and represents which children desire it by a bipartite graph. It measures communication rounds in CONGEST, where messages have bounded size. Its restricted model, communication cost and growing approximation factor differ from this centralized target; the paper’s separate discussion still identifies unrestricted allocation as open.

cards.title: Randomized truthful unrelated-machine scheduling
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors as the integer number of machines \(m\to\infty\), the optimal worst-case expected-makespan ratio \(R(m)\) of truthful-in-expectation mechanisms for unrelated-machine scheduling. For each \(m\ge2\), the mechanism must handle every finite job count \(n\ge1\) and every matrix of finite nonnegative real processing times. It may use payments and arbitrary correlated random assignments, with no computational or communication restriction.
\[R(m)=\inf_{M\in\mathcal M_m}\ \sup_{\substack{n\ge1,\ t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{OPT}(t)>0}}
\frac{\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]}{\operatorname{OPT}(t)}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_m\) consists of the families satisfying the incentive and zero-optimum conditions below. The question includes deciding whether \(R(m)=\Theta(1)\), but a negative answer to that special possibility alone does not determine the requested asymptotic order.
cards.definitions:
Jobs, machines and private costs. Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). There are \(m\ge2\) machines and \(n\ge1\) indivisible jobs. Machine \(i\) has a private type \(t_i=(t_{i1},\ldots,t_{in})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\). Executing a set \(S\subseteq[n]\) costs it \(\sum_{j\in S}t_{ij}\). All entries are finite; zero is allowed. The times on different machines and jobs have no promised relation. Every job is assigned exactly once, and all jobs assigned to one machine are executed sequentially. There are no release times, precedences, eligibility restrictions, migration, preemption or interactions between different jobs' costs.

Direct mechanisms. Reports have the same domain as types. For each report matrix \(b\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\), a mechanism specifies numbers
\[q_\sigma(b)\ge0\quad(\sigma:[n]\to[m]),\qquad\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(b)=1,\]
and a finite real expected payment \(p_i(b)\in\mathbb R\) to each machine. Thus the outcome at each fixed report is a distribution on the finite set of \(m^n\) assignments. Define the marginal assignment probability
\[x_{ij}(b)=\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(j)=i}q_\sigma(b).\]
The numbers \(q_\sigma(b)\) may be arbitrary reals, and assignments of different jobs need not be independent. Payments can be deterministic amounts \(p_i(b)\): allowing random payments with finite expectations makes no difference to the risk-neutral utility or objective here. Positive payments are received by the machine. No individual rationality, budget balance, sign restriction, transfer bound, anonymity or task-independence condition is imposed.

Truthfulness in expectation. For every machine \(i\), true type \(t_i\), alternative report \(b_i\), and fixed reports \(b_{-i}\) of all other machines, require
\[p_i(t_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{-i})
\ \ge\ p_i(b_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{-i}).\]
This is the dominant-strategy condition for expected payment minus true processing cost. Only one agent's report changes in this comparison. There is no prior distribution on types, expectation over other players' reports, or assumption that those reports are honest. The expectation is over the mechanism's own allocation randomness. Truthfulness of each deterministic rule obtained by fixing a random seed is not required.

Performance. When the report matrix equals the true matrix \(t\), an assignment has makespan
\[C(\sigma,t)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}t_{ij},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(t)=\min_{\sigma:[n]\to[m]}C(\sigma,t).\]
The expectation in the formal statement is the finite sum \(\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(t)C(\sigma,t)\). It is the expected maximum load, not the maximum of the expected loads. Payments do not enter the makespan. The optimum uses the same machines and jobs with full knowledge of the true processing times. For every \(t\) with \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=0\), an admissible mechanism must have expected makespan zero; division by zero is omitted from the displayed supremum. All positive-optimum instances and all job counts are included, with no additive error term.

Optimization over mechanisms. For a fixed \(m\), a family \(M=(M_{m,n})_{n\ge1}\) belongs to \(\mathcal M_m\) precisely when each member has the stated domain and satisfies truthfulness and the zero-optimum condition at every report profile. Its supremum ratio may be infinite. The infimum is finite because a truthful minimum-total-cost allocation has ratio at most \(m\), so \(1\le R(m)\le m\). A single family must meet its ratio simultaneously for every \(n\) and \(t\); it cannot be chosen after the true instance is known. Different job counts and machine counts may have different rules, and no uniform finite program, computability, representation or time bound is required. The selected problem is an incentive-theoretic extremum over mathematical rules on real reports. A bit encoding or efficient sampling requirement would change that class.

Attainment and asymptotics. The infimum need not be attained. To establish \(R(m)\le u\), it is enough to have admissible families with ratios at most \(u+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). The constants in the requested asymptotic comparison must be independent of \(m\), \(n\), and all processing times. The finite distribution on assignments at each individual report must not be confused with a report-independent finite or countable distribution over entire deterministic truthful mechanisms; the latter is an additional restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a positive asymptotic scale \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), constants \(a,b>0\), and an integer \(m_0\ge2\), with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[a f(m)\le R(m)\le b f(m)\qquad\text{for every integer }m\ge m_0.\]
The scale must specify the growth rate by an unambiguous mathematical description, not merely rename \(R\) or its defining optimization. Both bounds must apply to the full stated type domain, every job count and the full truthful-in-expectation class. Upper bounds may use families approaching an unattained infimum; lower bounds must constrain all admissible mechanisms, with no hidden computational, independence or distributional hypothesis.

A constant upper bound would suffice together with the universal lower bound one. Proving only unboundedness, improving one bound without a matching scale, or settling universal truthfulness, a fixed machine count, a fixed job count, fractional makespan or a Bayesian variant does not meet this criterion. Constant-factor asymptotic precision is the selected target; the numerical absolute-error convention is not an additive tolerance on asymptotic notation.

Matching asymptotic bounds would show whether expected-utility incentives can overcome the linear loss now known for deterministic truthful scheduling.

context_blocks.text: A machine can report a different processing-time vector to reduce the work it receives. Payments give the scheduler a way to counteract that incentive. Because a machine can be fast on one job and slow on another, its type is multidimensional; a single reported speed describes a substantially different model. The goal here measures the schedule at honest reports, while honesty must be optimal even when other machines report arbitrary vectors.

Total processing cost and makespan impose different objectives. A truthful minimum-total-cost allocation assigns each job to a cheapest machine, with appropriate payments. Its makespan is at most its total cost, which is at most the total cost of an optimal makespan assignment and hence at most \(m\operatorname{OPT}(t)\). This explains a universal factor \(m\). With complete information and unlimited computation, an optimal makespan assignment exists; the issue in this card is the additional incentive constraint.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that no deterministic truthful mechanism improves the worst-case factor \(m\). The result was posted in 2023 and published online in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It settles the deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture without a computational hardness assumption. It does not give the same lower bound for truthfulness in expectation.

Universal truthfulness means that the mechanism samples a deterministic truthful rule from a report-independent distribution. Truthfulness in expectation asks only that honest reporting maximize expected utility and permits a larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira prove the lower bound \(2-1/m\) for this larger class. Their theorem allows arbitrary finite processing times, including zero, and is independent of computational limitations.

Lu and Yu give the general truthful-in-expectation guarantee \((m+5)/2\). Together with the deterministic upper bound and the unrestricted randomized lower bound, the inspected literature gives
\[2-\frac1m\le R(m)\le\min\left\{m,\frac{m+5}{2}\right\}.\]
Thus the general gap remains between a constant and a linear function. The same WINE paper reports a linear lower bound under its task-independence restriction; that restricted conclusion cannot be transferred to the whole class defining \(R\).

Correlations matter even when every individual assignment probability is fixed. Take \(m\) unit jobs on \(m\) machines, with every processing time equal to one. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly chosen machine gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\) and makespan \(m\). Assigning the jobs by a uniformly chosen bijection also gives \(x_{ij}=1/m\), but makespan one. Both have expected load one on every machine. Expected utilities depend only on the marginal probabilities and expected payments, whereas expected makespan also depends on the joint assignment distribution.

cards.title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) and one uniform deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol which, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every profile of \(n\) nonatomic additive cake valuations, makes at most \(Cn^d\) queries and produces a partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) of the entire cake satisfying
\[
 \mu_i(A_i)\ge\mu_i(A_j)\qquad\text{for every }1\le i,j\le n?
\]
Every allocated piece may be a finite union of intervals. The allocation must be complete and exactly envy-free on every profile and for every valid choice of cut-query responses.
cards.definitions:
The cake is \([0,1]\). Agent \(i\)'s valuation \(\mu_i\) is an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure: it is nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu_i([0,1])=1\), and \(\mu_i(\{x\})=0\) for every point \(x\). A piece is a finite union of intervals, with endpoints assigned consistently to make the pieces disjoint. Endpoints have zero value for every agent. Measures need not have densities, and there is no bound on density, number of breakpoints or description complexity. No distribution over profiles is assumed.

The protocol receives \(n\) and accesses valuations only through these exact oracles:

\(\operatorname{Eval}(i,x,y)\), for known marks \(0\le x\le y\le1\), returns \(\mu_i([x,y])\).

\(\operatorname{Cut}(i,x,\alpha)\), for a known mark \(x\) and a requested real value \(0\le\alpha\le\mu_i([x,1])\), returns some \(y\in[x,1]\) such that \(\mu_i([x,y])=\alpha\). This returned coordinate becomes a known mark. Initially only \(0\) and \(1\) are known. Nonatomicity guarantees existence of an answer. If an interval has zero value, a cut may have several valid positions; every such response must preserve the guarantee. The protocol must issue only valid queries.

Each evaluation or cut call counts as one query. The protocol may combine interval values by additivity and use previously learned values without paying again. It may query one agent at a mark obtained from another. The final allocation must use endpoints among the known marks; arbitrary newly guessed endpoints are not available as free cuts.

Uniformity means one finite program for all \(n\). Between queries it may use integer computation, store and copy exact real answers, perform real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero number, and compare real numbers exactly. Its program has rational real constants and may perform arbitrary finite loops and finite searches. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; no time, memory or bit-precision bound is imposed on this local computation. It must nevertheless terminate after finitely many operations on every allowed execution. This specifies a query model with exact real arithmetic, not a Turing computation of the digits of arbitrary valuation reals.

The output lists, for each agent, finitely many intervals with known endpoints. Their union covers \([0,1]\), and no interior point belongs to two agents' pieces. Shared boundary points are assigned to one incident piece. Empty pieces are allowed, but no positive-length residue may be discarded, even if all agents value it at zero.

Envy-freeness compares all pieces using the evaluating agent's own measure. It requires every displayed inequality exactly, with no additive or multiplicative fairness error. It does not require a connected piece per agent or impose any incentive-compatibility condition. The query bound is worst-case over both valuation profiles and valid oracle responses. There is no randomization or favorable-profile exception.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one protocol and constants satisfying the statement, with proofs of query validity, termination, complete allocation, exact envy-freeness and the uniform polynomial query bound; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence claim in the specified model.

A protocol with an arbitrary finite bound depending on \(n\), a polynomial average-case or approximate-fairness guarantee, or a protocol leaving cake unallocated is insufficient. A lower bound for one particular procedure does not rule out all polynomial-query protocols. This is an existence question about an exact fairness property and an asymptotic resource bound, so numerical approximation of envy does not meet the answer criterion.
cards.why: The question asks how much preference information is necessary to divide a continuous resource exactly without anyone preferring another person’s share. A polynomial query bound would separate the information needed for fairness from the enormous bounds in existing general protocols.

cards.definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of \(n\ge 1\) voters and C of \(m\ge 1\) candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each \(v\in V\). A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on \(V\cup C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)\ge 0\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points, with a≻_v b implying \(d(v,a)\le d(v,b)\). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair \((E,d)\). The social cost \(SC_{d}(a)=\sum_{v\in V} d(v,a)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=\min _{a}\in C SC_{d}(a)\). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery \(p=f(E)\), where \(p_{a}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{a} p_{a}=1\). Its expected cost is \(\sum_{a} p_{a} SC_{d}(a)\). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define \(Dist(f)=\inf\){\(D\ge 1\): for every E and every consistent \(d, \sum_{a} f(E)_{a} SC_{d}(a)\le D\cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{d}\)}, taking \(\inf \varnothing =+\infty\). This inequality requires zero expected cost if \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=0\) and avoids dividing by zero. Set \(D*=\inf _{f} Dist(f)\), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.

context_blocks.title: Rankings hide the size of a preference
context_blocks.text: Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

context_blocks.title: What randomization changes
context_blocks.text: If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively \(3- 2p\) and \(1+2p\). At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

context_blocks.title: The old value-2 conjecture is false
context_blocks.text: Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

context_blocks.title: Restricted rules answer different questions
context_blocks.text: A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

context_blocks.title: Why this constant matters
context_blocks.text: D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.

cards.context:
Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively \(3- 2p\) and \(1+2p\). At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.

cards.title: Nonemptiness of the approval core
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
For every pair of integers \(n,m\ge1\), every integer \(1\le k\le m\), and every approval profile \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) with \(A_i\subseteq[m]\), is there a committee \(W\subseteq[m]\) of size \(k\) such that no nonempty coalition \(S\subseteq[n]\) and alternative committee \(T\subseteq[m]\) satisfy both
\[n|T|\le k|S|\quad\text{and}\quad\forall i\in S,\ |A_i\cap T|>|A_i\cap W|?\]
cards.definitions: For an integer \(r\ge1\), \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\). There are \(n\) equally weighted voters and \(m\) distinct, indivisible candidates of unit cost. Voter \(i\) approves exactly the set \(A_i\) and assigns utility \(u_i(U)=|A_i\cap U|\) to a committee \(U\). Approval sets may be empty. The chosen committee contains exactly \(k\) distinct candidates. A nonempty voter coalition \(S\) can afford any set of candidates \(T\) with \(|T|\le k|S|/n\), using the Hare quota without additional rounding beyond this inequality. It blocks \(W\) if every one of its members obtains a strictly larger approval count from \(T\) than from \(W\). The two committees may overlap; \(T\) need not be contained in \(W\) or in its complement. Each candidate may appear at most once. The core is the collection of committees with no such blocking coalition and alternative. The question concerns existence, without an efficiency requirement for finding or certifying a committee.

context_blocks.text: The core formalizes proportional group representation: a coalition should not be able to use its share of the available seats to make all its members better represented. Because a selected candidate serves all voters who approve it, this is a public committee problem rather than a partition of goods among individual recipients.

The fractional core is known to be nonempty, but fractional selection can split candidates. Allowing unlimited copies changes the model as well. Neither guarantee establishes existence for a set of indivisible candidates, each selected at most once.

Goel, Jiang and Zhou explicitly state that unrestricted discrete-core nonemptiness remains open. Their August 2026 preprint reports a positive result for at most eight equally weighted voters using exhaustive computational verification; that reported result is a restricted case and its computations were not independently audited here.
The TCS+ talk by Gölz presents proportional representation and highlights the unit-cost approval setting as a central unresolved existence question.

cards.why: Core nonemptiness is a foundational feasibility question for proportional representation: can all voter coalitions be satisfied simultaneously when seats are indivisible? A resolution would identify whether the strongest basic coalition-stability demand is universally compatible with approval committee selection.

cards.definitions: There are exactly three agents, indexed 1,2,3, and \(m\ge 0\) goods indexed by \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\). The input gives m and each value \(v_{i},g=p_{i},g/q_{i},g\) with integers \(p_{i},g\ge 0\) and \(q_{i},g>0\) encoded in binary. N is the total bit length of this explicit table and its delimiters. For any bundle \(S\subseteq [m], v_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}v_{i},g\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_{1},A_{2},A_{3})\) of \([m]\); bundles may be empty. The output assigns each good one owner in \(\{1,2,3\}\). It is EFX if \(v_{i}(A_{i})\ge v_{i}(A_{j}\setminus \{g\})\) for every \(i,j\in \{1,2,3\}\) and every \(g\in A_{j}\), including goods with \(v_{i},g=0\). The removed good is evaluated by agent i. An empty \(A_{j}\) gives no inequality; a singleton leaves the empty bundle of value zero. Removal is hypothetical and does not discard a good from the output. Values may have arbitrary magnitudes and denominators. The algorithm is uniform, deterministic and always correct, with ordinary bit-operation cost and no oracle, payments or divisible goods. Its running time must be polynomial in N, not in the numeric values.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives an algorithm and proves completeness, every EFX inequality, and a worst-case polynomial bit bound on all inputs. A negative answer proves that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. Existence alone is already established for this three-agent additive model; a particular unfair allocation, pseudopolynomial runtime or a relaxed fairness guarantee does not answer the computational question.

context_blocks.title: Every possible removed good matters
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

context_blocks.title: Existence has already been proved
context_blocks.text: Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

context_blocks.title: Why pseudopolynomial time is insufficient
context_blocks.text: A value as large as \(2^{\mathrm{L}}\) needs only \(\mathrm{L}+1\) binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including \(2/3-\mathrm{EFX}\) for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.

cards.definitions: An instance has \(n\ge 1\) agents, \(m\ge 0\) indivisible chores, and finite real costs \(c_{i},g\ge 0\). Agent i assigns a bundle \(S\subseteq [m]\) the additive cost \(c_{i}(S)=\sum _{g\in S}c_{i},g\); lower cost is better. Let \(\Pi _{n}([m])\) be the finite set of ordered partitions of \([m]\) into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define \(\mu _{i}=\min _{(\mathrm{P}_{1},\ldots ,\mathrm{P}_{n})\in \Pi _{n}([m])} \max _{1\le j\le n} c_{i}(\mathrm{P}_{j})\). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to \(\Pi _{n}([m])\): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when \(\mu _{i}=0\), without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \alpha *|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

cards.title: Optimal universal approximation factor for EFX
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Determine the universal additive-goods EFX approximation constant
\[\alpha_* = \sup\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists A\in\mathcal A_{n,m},\ A\text{ is }\alpha\text{-EFX for }v\}.\]
Here \(n,m\) are integers, \(\mathcal A_{n,m}\) is the set of complete allocations of \(m\) goods to \(n\) agents, and \(\alpha\)-EFX uses the positive-good convention defined below. The requested benchmark precision is absolute error at most \(1/100\): supply a real number \(a\) and prove \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). This is an existence constant with unrestricted allocation computation, not a polynomial-time approximation threshold.
cards.why: This constant measures how much of the demanding EFX fairness comparison can always be guaranteed when all indivisible goods must be assigned. It gives a quantitative target even if exact EFX existence is unresolved. Its scope is every number of agents and every additive valuation profile, so improvements for special structures do not alone determine the universal guarantee.

cards.definitions:
Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) for integers \(k\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is a finite nonnegative real number giving agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\). For a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\), its value is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). No normalization, strict positivity, integrality, rationality, number-of-types or agreement-on-ordering assumption is imposed on values.

A complete allocation \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is an ordered partition of \([m]\): the bundles are pairwise disjoint and their union is all of \([m]\). Empty bundles are allowed. There are no payments, negative-valued chores, fractional goods, discarded goods or additional efficiency constraints.

For \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), the allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX if
\[\forall i,j\in[n]\ \forall g\in A_j:\quad v_{ig}>0\ \Longrightarrow\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\}).\]
Both the test of whether the removed good has positive value and the bundle comparison use the potentially envious agent \(i\)'s values. If every good of \(A_j\) has value zero to \(i\), there is no constraint for that pair. If the remaining bundle has value zero, the inequality is automatically satisfied. This is Definition 6 of the source survey. The stronger per-allocation convention often called EFX-zero tests also removed goods of zero value; the card does not silently substitute that convention.

The universally feasible set in the supremum is nonempty, because it includes zero, and is bounded above by one by definition. The constant is dimensionless. Its quantifier order allows a different allocation for each valuation matrix; no single common partition must serve all profiles. Neither an efficient algorithm nor any oracle-access restriction is part of the existence guarantee.

For a fixed finite instance \(v\), one can equivalently define \(\beta(v)\) as the largest \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) for which some complete allocation is \(\alpha\)-EFX. This maximum exists: there are finitely many allocations, and each has a closed interval of feasible factors. Then \(\alpha_*\) is the infimum of these \(\beta(v)\) over all permitted instance sizes and profiles. There need not be one instance attaining this infimum. This equivalent definition makes the universal lower-bound and worst-instance upper-bound meanings explicit.

Exact equality \(\alpha_*=1\) is equivalent to existence of a complete EFX allocation for every additive instance: for each fixed instance, finitely many allocations and closed inequalities prevent loss of the endpoint. A numerical answer within \(1/100\) need not decide that exact equality. The present acceptance tolerance measures the numerical constant and does not relax the definition of \(\alpha\)-EFX itself.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\alpha_*|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) containing \(\alpha_*\) qualifies via its midpoint; an exact value also qualifies. Bounds must concern all finite nonnegative additive instances and complete allocations under the stated positive-good convention. A universal construction proves only a lower bound on the constant unless accompanied by sufficient upper information. An upper bound may be established without a worst instance attaining the infimum. Restricted numbers of agents, partial allocations, nonadditive counterexamples, or guarantees allowing removal of multiple goods do not by themselves determine this constant. A simulation or an unproved decimal estimate is insufficient.

Their definition tests every removed good, including zero-valued goods, so their guarantee also implies the positive-good condition here. The EC 2024 work establishes \(2/3\)-EFX under restrictions including at most seven agents or at most three common value levels. cards.definitions: The cake is \([0,1]\). Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure \(\mu _{i}\): values are nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu _{i}([0,1])=1\), and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: \(Eval(i,x,y)\) returns \(\mu _{i}([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a)\), for \(0\le a\le \mu _{i}([x,1])\), returns \(y\ge x\) with \(\mu _{i}([x,y])=a\). Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge 1/n\) for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. In this question each \(A_{i}\) must be one interval, up to ownership of its endpoints. The intervals may have gaps between them, and the residue \([0,1]\setminus \bigcup _{i}A_{i}\) may be discarded. Envy is compared with other agents’ assigned intervals, not with the residue. Count every Eval and Cut call as one query. The bound \(B_{n}\) depends only on the fixed n and its protocol, never on the valuation profile or oracle responses. The statement permits a separate finite protocol for each n; it does not require \(B_{n}\) to be polynomial, and does not add an algorithm that generates all \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a bounded protocol for every fixed \(n\ge 4\), or prove that for at least one fixed \(n\ge 4\) no deterministic protocol and finite bound satisfy the stated guarantees. Existence of a suitable division alone, a procedure that merely converges to one, approximate proportionality, or allowing an agent several intervals does not meet this target.

context_blocks.title: Fairness with one usable piece
context_blocks.text: A connected share is a single interval, as in a continuous appointment slot or one tract of land. Envy-freeness says each person prefers her own assigned interval to anyone else’s. Proportionality additionally protects the amount she receives: at least one n-th of her value for the whole resource.

context_blocks.title: Why disposal changes the question
context_blocks.text: With disposal, giving everyone nothing is envy-free. For example, agents with identical uniform values can each receive an interval of length \(1/(2n)\), leaving half the cake unused; none envies another, but all receive less than their proportional share. The exact \(1/n\) requirement excludes such wasteful outcomes.

context_blocks.title: The connected impossibility has a specific scope
context_blocks.text: Stromquist proves that no finite protocol can always allocate the entire cake envy-freely with one interval per agent once \(n\ge 3\). This assumes complete allocation. Allowing residue is the change studied here, so that theorem does not refute this question.

context_blocks.title: Known partial-allocation guarantees
context_blocks.text: Waste Makes Haste gives a bounded connected envy-free proportional protocol for three agents in its density model. For four agents its connected guarantee is \(1/7\) instead of the required \(1/4\). Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded connected partial allocation with a \(1/(3n)\) value guarantee in general. These results motivate the question but do not supply exact proportionality for all \(n\ge 4\).

context_blocks.title: Later progress allows fragmented shares
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports a single-exponential query bound for complete envy-free allocation. Complete envy-freeness implies proportionality, but the output may contain multiple intervals per agent. It therefore does not answer this connected-piece question.

cards.title: Universal Condorcet dimension
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Determine the universal Condorcet dimension \(d_*\): the least positive integer \(d\) such that for every pair of integers \(n,m\ge1\) and every profile \((\succ_1,\ldots,\succ_n)\) of strict total orders on \([m]\), there exists a nonempty set \(W\subseteq[m]\) with \(|W|\le d\) and
\[\forall a\in[m]\setminus W,\qquad\bigl|\{i\in[n]:\ \forall w\in W,\ a\succ_i w\}\bigr|<\frac n2.\]
The target is measured in number of candidates, with absolute acceptance error at most \(1/100\).
cards.definitions: For \(r\ge1\), \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\). There are \(n\) equally weighted voters and \(m\) distinct candidates. Each voter ranks all candidates without ties, and \(a\succ_i w\) means that voter \(i\) places \(a\) above \(w\). A Condorcet winning set in this card is a nonempty committee \(W\) such that, for each outsider \(a\), strictly more than half the voters prefer at least one member of \(W\) to \(a\). Different voters may prefer different committee members. Equivalently, strictly fewer than half rank the outsider above every member, as in the displayed formula. The strict inequality is intentional, including for an even electorate. The chosen committee may depend on the entire profile and need not be found efficiently. The least universal bound \(d_*\) ranges over all finite electorate and candidate sizes. Its existence as a finite positive integer follows from the known bound of five; if \(m\) is smaller, taking all candidates is allowed. This is a numerical universal bound, not a function of a fixed election and not a tournament domination number.

context_blocks.text: A single Condorcet winner may fail to exist because majority preferences can cycle. Allowing a small set changes the comparison: each voter compares an outsider with that voter’s own most preferred selected candidate. The question asks for the smallest committee size that always provides a strict voter majority against every outsider.

Charikar, Lassota, Ramakrishnan, Vetta and Wang prove that six candidates always suffice and describe examples for which two do not. Their Question 1 uses the strict-majority convention retained in this card; the exact universal threshold remains undetermined.

The 2025 preprint A few good choices improves the upper bound to five. Although it defines undominance with a weak inequality, its Theorem 1 gives a five-candidate bound at most \(1/3+(2/3)^5=113/243<1/2\) for the fraction preferring any outsider. Thus the stated theorem also gives the strict guarantee used here.
The April 2026 study Is Four Enough? still reports the gap \(3\le d_*\le5\). It supplies further evidence for smaller bounds, rather than a proof that determines the universal dimension.

cards.why: This determines the smallest universally sufficient relaxation of a Condorcet winner in ranked elections. The recent constant-size existence results leave a small but fundamental gap about how many representatives are needed to obtain majority acceptance independently of election size.
