cards.title: Universal maximin-share approximation for additive goods
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine the universal maximin-share approximation constant for additive indivisible goods, \[\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}=\sup\bigl\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in\Pi_n([m])\ \forall i\in[n],\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,\mu_i(v)\bigr\}.\] Here \(n,m\) range over integers, \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\), and \(\mu_i(v)=\max_{(P_1,\ldots,P_n)\in\Pi_n([m])}\min_{j\in[n]}v_i(P_j)\). The benchmark asks for this one dimensionless constant with absolute error at most \(1/100\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of the error bound.
cards.why: Maximin share gives each agent a fairness benchmark determined by their own values, independent of how the other agents evaluate the goods. These personal guarantees can conflict when objects are indivisible. The universal constant measures the unavoidable loss from satisfying all agents simultaneously, separating a limitation of fairness itself from a limitation of available algorithms. It is a central quantitative threshold for additive fair division, with significance across instances and arbitrary numbers of participants.
cards.status_note: The January 2026 source explicitly poses this constant. Checked primary statements through 14 September 2026 give the published upper bound 39/40 and a revised-preprint lower-bound claim of 7/9, still far apart at benchmark precision. The 7 September 2026 revision reports a corrected bug; this review verifies its stated scope, not every step of its proof. No matching determination was found in the bounded search.

progress.text: Feige, Sapir and Tauber, Theorem 1, prove the universal upper bound \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\le39/40\) using three agents and nine goods. Their Theorem 3 is tight only within that restricted instance size.

Heidari et al., Theorem 3.1, establish the \(10/13\) additive-goods guarantee. This is the value stated in their own manuscript, rather than the \(7/9\) value grouped with the citation on the problem-list page.
The TCS Open Problems entry asks for the best universal maximin-share approximation and links the additive-goods literature.

Huang and Zhou’s arXiv version 2 states a \(7/9\) guarantee through Theorem 3.1 and the general-instance correspondence in Lemma 2.4; Theorem 10.4 concerns \((7/9-\varepsilon)\)-MMS computation. The revision notice reports a corrected bug. The claimed interval still does not determine the benchmark constant within \(1/100\).

sentences: Each agent’s maximin share is the best value they can secure by partitioning the goods and receiving a least-valued bundle.
The target is the largest fraction of those personal shares that can always be met simultaneously for nonnegative additive valuations.
It ranges over all finite numbers of agents and indivisible goods, with equal entitlements and no sharing.
Determining this constant would quantify the inherent loss of fairness caused by indivisibility, independently of computational efficiency.
The card requires a Lean-certified absolute error of at most one hundredth and records the precise versions and limits of the known bounds.

cards.definitions: Write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). The set \(\Pi_n([m])\) consists of ordered \(n\)-tuples of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is all of \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed. Each item belongs to exactly one agent, with no splitting, sharing, disposal, payments or externalities. Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is an arbitrary finite nonnegative real value, and values of bundles are additive. Every agent has the same entitlement; the number of agents determining each maximin share is the original \(n\). The partition maximizing \(\mu_i(v)\) is chosen separately for each agent using that agent’s valuations. Its maximum exists because there are finitely many partitions. If \(\mu_i(v)=0\), the corresponding approximation requirement is simply \(v_i(A_i)\ge0\); no ratio with a zero denominator is taken. Valuations need not be identical, normalized, strictly positive or drawn from a finite value set. The allocation may depend on the entire instance. No runtime bound, incentive condition, randomness model or finite encoding of the real entries is imposed, because the target concerns mathematical existence rather than efficient computation. The supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\), since the feasible set contains zero. The question covers all finite agent and item counts simultaneously, rather than the best guarantee for any one fixed \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical specification of one, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}|\le1/100\), using exactly the universal domain and maximin-share definition above. A proved interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. One-sided guarantees, counterexamples without a matching sufficiently close lower bound, empirical searches, or results only for a fixed number of agents do not meet the criterion. Determination of the exact supremum is welcome but not required; the submitted approximation need not itself be a universally attainable allocation ratio. The existing gap between \(7/9\) and \(39/40\) is wider than the permitted interval.

context_blocks.text: An agent can imagine partitioning the goods into as many bundles as there are participants and then receiving a least-valued bundle. Optimizing that personal partition defines the maximin share. Actual allocation must respect all agents at once, although their best partitions and their rankings of the goods can be different.

The source asks for the best universal approximation and points to results for additive goods. Those linked papers fix the intended valuation class and distinguish it from chores or more general set valuations. The card makes this source-supported interpretation explicit and retains an existence target, without adding a demand for an efficient allocation algorithm.

Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-good instance in which every allocation leaves someone with at most \(39/40\) of their maximin share. This bounds the universal constant from above even though its definition includes arbitrarily large instances. Their tight result for that particular pair of agent and item counts is not a tight universal guarantee.

Heidari, Kaviani, Seddighin and Shahrezaei prove a \(10/13\) guarantee. Huang and Zhou’s revised September 2026 manuscript states a \(7/9\) existence guarantee and a fully polynomial approximation scheme for slightly smaller ratios. These are distinct results: the problem-list entry groups their citations under \(7/9\), but the Heidari et al. paper itself states \(10/13\).

The Huang–Zhou revision explicitly reports correction of a bug and substantial rewriting of the proof. Its version and theorem scope are recorded here, without certifying the full proof independently. Computational approximation schemes and stronger results under restrictions on the number of agents remain different from determining the unrestricted existence constant.

cards.title: Polynomial-time EF1 and Pareto-optimal goods allocation
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicitly given instance of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations, outputs an allocation that is both envy-free up to one good (EF1) and Pareto optimal (PO)?

Precisely, do there exist one algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), and matrix
\[
(v_{ig})_{i\in[n],\,g\in[m]}\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times m},
\]
\(A\) outputs a complete integral allocation satisfying the two conditions below in at most \(C(L+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(L\) is the full binary input length? The same program, constant and exponent must work for every number of agents and goods.
cards.why: Fairness and efficiency can each be obtained quickly, and an allocation satisfying both always exists. The unresolved computational question asks whether the two can be reconciled without time proportional to numerical value magnitudes or an exponent growing with the number of participants. It is a basic boundary between existence and efficient construction in discrete fair division.
cards.status_note: The 2022 survey asks for polynomial-time EF1 and PO allocation under additive goods valuations. The May 2026 publication of Mahara’s fixed-agent algorithm explicitly retains the general question, as does the March 2026 balanced-allocation paper. No unrestricted polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem was found in the bounded later-work review.

sentences: The task is to divide indivisible goods among agents whose nonnegative values add across goods.
EF1 allows each agent’s envy of another bundle to disappear after the hypothetical removal of at most one good.
Pareto optimality forbids any reassignment that improves one agent without hurting another.

Known pseudo-polynomial and fixed-agent algorithms do not settle this general bit-time requirement.

cards.definitions:
Write \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) distinct goods. Each good is indivisible and must be assigned to exactly one agent. An allocation is a tuple \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) of disjoint subsets of \([m]\) whose union is \([m]\). Empty bundles are permitted.

Agent \(i\)'s value for a bundle \(S\) is
\[
v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}.
\]
All entries are nonnegative; zero entries, zero-valued agents and goods valued at zero by everyone are allowed. Values depend only on the agent's own bundle. There are no monetary transfers, capacities, equal-bundle-size requirements, unequal entitlements or restrictions on which agent may receive which good.

The allocation \(X\) is EF1 when
\[
\forall i,j\in[n]\ \exists S\subseteq X_j,\quad
|S|\le1\quad\text{and}\quad v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(X_j\setminus S).
\]
The removal is only hypothetical and does not discard an allocated good. The set \(S\) may depend on the ordered pair \(i,j\). Allowing \(S=\varnothing\) covers the case of no envy and empty envied bundles. The condition asks for some removable good, rather than every removable good; the latter is a stronger fairness condition.

The allocation \(X\) is PO if there is no other complete integral allocation \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)\) such that
\[
\bigl(\forall i\in[n],\ v_i(Y_i)\ge v_i(X_i)\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(\exists j\in[n],\ v_j(Y_j)>v_j(X_j)\bigr).
\]
The competing allocation may reassign any number of goods, and need not be EF1. PO therefore excludes every integral Pareto improvement, not just a local exchange or another fair allocation. The target uses integral alternatives. Fractional Pareto optimality, which also excludes improvements obtained by splitting goods, is stronger and is not separately required.

The input explicitly lists \(n,m\) and every matrix entry in row-major order. Use unary headers \(1^n0\,1^m0\), followed by each rational as \(p_{ig}/q_{ig}\) with integers \(p_{ig}\ge0\), \(q_{ig}\ge1\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), encode \(a+1\) by its \(b\)-bit binary representation preceded by \(1^b0\). Use this code for every numerator and denominator, requiring no trailing bits. Fractions need not be reduced. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits, including all headers and rational entries.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one fixed finite program, read-only input and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes the cells under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell. All parsing, arithmetic, preprocessing and output are charged; no valuation oracle, advice or randomness is available. The output lists the receiving agent for each good, in increasing good order, using \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits per label. For \(m=0\), the empty output denotes the unique allocation. Malformed inputs must be rejected within the same polynomial bound.

Polynomial time is measured in the bit length, not in the magnitudes of the values. A bound polynomial in a largest integer value can be exponential in \(L\). Conversely, the target does not demand strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. Rational inputs do not add an essential promise: multiplying all values of an agent by the product of that agent's denominators produces nonnegative integers of polynomial bit length and preserves both EF1 and PO.

The requested output must satisfy both conditions exactly. This is an algorithm-existence proposition, not a numerical target, so absolute \(1/100\) accuracy does not allow an envy violation or a Pareto improvement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial bit-time bound and proofs that every output is a complete allocation satisfying EF1 and PO; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. An existence theorem for allocations without the running-time guarantee, a pseudo-polynomial algorithm, an algorithm for each fixed number of agents with a growing exponent, or an approximation to either output condition is insufficient. A conditional hardness theorem is only a conditional obstruction unless its required complexity separation is also proved. Hardness of maximizing Nash welfare or of verifying PO does not by itself prove hardness of finding some EF1 and PO allocation.

cards.formal: Does every finite instance of indivisible mixed-item allocation with \(n\ge3\) agents and arbitrary real additive utilities admit a complete allocation that is both envy-free up to one item (EF1) and Pareto optimal (PO)? The item removed to eliminate an agent’s envy may come from the envied bundle or from the envious agent’s own bundle, with at most one item removed in total.
cards.why: Fairness and efficiency can conflict when an indivisible item benefits one participant and burdens another. This question asks whether one standard minimal relaxation of envy is always compatible with the absence of a Pareto improvement. Resolving it would determine whether a central fairness–efficiency guarantee survives unrestricted mixed valuations beyond the now-understood pure-goods and pure-chores existence settings.

The checked September 2026 weighted-fairness results and November 2025 pure-chores theorem do not settle this target. The search through 2026-09-15 was bounded and does not certify that no later resolution exists.

cards.definitions: The agents are \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the items are \([m]\) for any integer \(m\ge0\). Each agent \(i\) has values \(v_{i,g}\in\mathbb R\), with no restrictions on their signs or magnitudes, and \(u_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{i,g}\) for every \(S\subseteq[m]\). The same item may have positive, zero or negative value to different agents. Agents have equal entitlements; no normalization of utility totals is imposed. An allocation \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is a partition of all items into pairwise disjoint bundles, which may be empty. Every item must be assigned exactly once. No disposal, monetary transfers or fractional assignment is permitted. Allocation \(A\) is EF1 if for every ordered pair of distinct agents \(i,j\), at least one of the following holds: \(u_i(A_i)\ge u_i(A_j)\); there exists \(g\in A_j\) such that \(u_i(A_i)\ge u_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\); or there exists \(g\in A_i\) such that \(u_i(A_i\setminus\{g\})\ge u_i(A_j)\). These alternatives remove at most one item from one of the two bundles for this comparison only; they do not change the allocation. In particular, removing one item from each bundle is not allowed. Allocation \(A\) is PO if no other complete integral allocation \(B\) satisfies \(u_i(B_i)\ge u_i(A_i)\) for every \(i\) and \(u_j(B_j)>u_j(A_j)\) for at least one \(j\). The quantifiers are \(\forall n\ge3\;\forall m\ge0\;\forall v\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\;\exists A\), with both properties required of the same \(A\). The target is existence; there is no polynomial-time computation or representation requirement for an allocation-selection rule.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal existence statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may specify a finite real-valued instance and prove that none of its complete integral allocations satisfies both defined properties. An existence theorem confined to pure goods, pure chores, two agents, restricted value magnitudes or a different envy relaxation does not prove the general statement. A computation-time bound is not additionally required.

For example, if i values her bundle at −4 and j’s at 2, and deleting one item from her own bundle raises its value to 2, that comparison satisfies EF1.

An arbitrary utility can satisfy \(u(\{a\})=u(\{b\})=1\) but \(u(\{a,b\})=- 3\). Each item is beneficial when received alone and harmful when added to the other. This is allowed by the question, so a fixed classification of every item as a good or chore would restrict the model.

The survey records EF1 existence for two agents with arbitrary utilities and for any number of agents under additive or doubly-monotonic utilities. Doubly-monotonic means that, for each agent, every item has a fixed nonnegative or nonpositive marginal effect in every bundle. Open Question 1 removes that restriction for three or more agents.

The AAAI 2026 paper proves related existence statements for a relaxation allowing one removal from each compared bundle, for nonnegative or nonpositive valuations. That may remove two items in a comparison. The present target allows at most one item in total and permits arbitrary real utility values.

cards.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and for each player \(i\) a nonempty explicitly enumerated action set \(A_i=\{1,\ldots,k_i\}\). Each edge \(\{i,j\}\), with \(i<j\), carries an explicitly listed matrix \(M_{ij}\in\mathbb Q^{k_i\times k_j}\). If its endpoints choose \(a\in A_i\) and \(b\in A_j\), both receive the same edge payoff \(M_{ij}(a,b)\). Set \(M_{ji}(b,a)=M_{ij}(a,b)\) for reverse orientation. Each player selects one action for all its incident edges and receives the sum of those edge payoffs; nonedges contribute zero. A mixed profile \(p=(p_i)_{i\in V}\) uses independent probability vectors \(p_i\) on \(A_i\). For a pure deviation \(a\in A_i\), write \[v_i(a,p_{-i})=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}\sum_{b\in A_j}p_j(b)M_{ij}(a,b),\qquad u_i(p)=\sum_{a\in A_i}p_i(a)v_i(a,p_{-i}).\] It is an exact Nash equilibrium when \(v_i(a,p_{-i})\le u_i(p)\) for every player \(i\) and every action \(a\). The required output explicitly lists nonnegative rational probabilities summing to one for each player. A pure profile is allowed as a degenerate mixed profile; neither full support nor a genuinely randomizing player is required. Vertices, edges and all actions are listed, and each payoff is encoded by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator with delimiters. Thus the input length \(N\) includes the action lists, graph and every payoff bit; no succinct payoff circuit is allowed. Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, no advice or oracles, and a bound \(C(N+1)^d\) on all valid inputs for constants \(C,d\) independent of the instance. Charge every bit operation and output bit. The target is exact equilibrium, with no approximation parameter or promise on payoff magnitudes, graph degree or action counts.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of the stated uniform polynomial-time algorithm, including termination, the full bit bound and exact equilibrium correctness, or of its logical negation. A hardness reduction under an unproved separation establishes only a conditional conclusion. A polynomial bound in numerical payoff magnitudes, a fixed graph or action-count special case, or an approximate-equilibrium algorithm without an exact guarantee does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Coordination is imposed locally: the two endpoints agree on the payoff of their shared interaction. A player with several neighbors must nevertheless choose one action that participates in all those interactions. Equal payoffs on each edge therefore do not mean that every player has the same total payoff on every full profile.

For example, on a three-vertex path, the middle player receives the sum from both edges, while each endpoint receives only its single edge payoff. The middle player can face conflicting preferences from its two interactions even though each separate interaction gives identical rewards to its two participants.

The 2014 Dagstuhl report attributes the network-coordination question to Rahul Savani and explicitly imposes equality in each edge’s payoff pair. The present card makes polynomial-time tractability the binary target of that broader complexity question; Cai and Daskalakis already explicitly ask whether this search problem is in P.

Cai and Daskalakis show that finding a pure equilibrium is complete for polynomial local search, abbreviated PLS, while finding any mixed equilibrium belongs to both PLS and the parity-based total-search class PPAD. Permitting mixed output changes the search task even though pure equilibria exist: hardness of finding a pure equilibrium alone does not classify the task that may return any mixed one.

The same primary source records that rational polymatrix games have mixed equilibria with rational probabilities and polynomial description length. Exact output is consequently meaningful in the bit model and is not obstructed by a need to print arbitrary irrational numbers.

Hollender, Maystre and Nagarajan prove hardness for two-team polymatrix games with coordination inside teams and zero-sum interactions between teams. Their result allows adversarial edges absent from this card, and therefore does not classify coordination-only games. Likewise, an equilibrium constrained to be symmetric is a different output requirement.

The question tests whether permitting players to randomize makes arbitrary networks of local common-interest interactions computationally tractable. The input restriction and the freedom to return any equilibrium both matter; neither general-game hardness nor the ease of a single two-player coordination game settles this network case.

cards.title: Pure positional Nash equilibria in reachability games
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Does every finite deterministic turn-based multiplayer game with a designated initial vertex and a reachability objective for each player admit a pure positional Nash equilibrium?

The equilibrium is evaluated from that one initial vertex. A unilateral deviating strategy may depend on the complete finite history, even though every strategy in the proposed equilibrium must depend only on the current vertex.
cards.why: A positional strategy stores no history and is directly implementable as one choice per vertex. The question asks whether all players can always make mutually stable choices of this form when their goals are to reach target sets, despite the extra power available to a deviating player who remembers the past.
cards.status_note: The MFCS 2026 paper gives randomized memoryless equilibria for a wider combination of objectives, but its conclusion explicitly leaves pure positional equilibrium existence open when all objectives are reachability. Its absorbing-target positive theorem imposes an extra restriction absent here. The selected ordinary equilibrium is required from one initial vertex, not simultaneously from all vertices.

cards.definitions:
Fix any integer \(k\ge1\). An arena consists of a nonempty finite vertex set \(V\), a directed edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), a partition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_k\), and an initial vertex \(v_0\in V\). Empty parts are allowed. Every vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. At a vertex in \(V_i\), player \(i\) chooses the next vertex along one outgoing edge. All players observe the full history. There are no simultaneous moves, random transitions or hidden information.

Player \(i\) has any target set \(T_i\subseteq V\), which may be empty or overlap other targets. Targets are not required to be absorbing: play may leave a target after reaching it. An infinite play \(\rho=v_0v_1v_2\cdots\) follows edges of \(E\). Its payoff to player \(i\) is
\[
u_i(\rho)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if }v_t\in T_i\text{ for some integer }t\ge0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Thus a visit at time zero counts, and visiting a target once suffices forever. No player has a safety, recurrence or parity objective.

A pure strategy for player \(i\) assigns a legal successor to each finite path whose last vertex lies in \(V_i\). It can use the entire path and has no memory or computability restriction. A pure positional strategy is a function \(\sigma_i:V_i\to V\) satisfying \((v,\sigma_i(v))\in E\) for every \(v\in V_i\); at every occurrence of that vertex it makes the same choice.

A profile \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k)\) determines one infinite play \(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma)\). It is a Nash equilibrium from \(v_0\) when, for every player \(i\) and every pure history-dependent strategy \(\tau_i\),
\[
u_i\bigl(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma)\bigr)
\ge
u_i\bigl(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma_{-i},\tau_i)\bigr).
\]
Here \((\sigma_{-i},\tau_i)\) replaces only player \(i\)'s strategy; every other player keeps the originally specified strategy, including at vertices not reached by the original play. A player already winning cannot improve. A losing player must have no unilateral way to reach its target.

The question quantifies over all finite arenas, all target sets, all player counts and every designated start, and asks for the existence of a positional profile for each such instance. The profile may depend on the start. It need not be an equilibrium from every vertex simultaneously or following every history, and no particular payoff vector is prescribed. No running-time bound or algorithm to find the profile is required. Randomized positional profiles do not meet the pure-strategy requirement. Allowing randomized deviations with expected binary payoffs would give the same equilibrium condition against a fixed pure profile: a positive probability of reaching a target entails a finite legal reaching history that can be followed by a pure deviation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every instance in the stated class has such a pure positional equilibrium, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may provide one finite arena, target sets and initial vertex together with a proof that every pure positional profile has a profitable unilateral deviation.

A counterexample using other objective types, stochastic transitions, a required payoff vector, or equilibrium simultaneously from every vertex does not settle this proposition. Existence of randomized memoryless profiles or pure profiles with memory does not prove it. Positive results restricted to absorbing targets do not cover the full target.

cards.definitions: The input explicitly lists vertices \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge0\), distinct nonempty hyperedges \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\subseteq2^V\), and, for each vertex, a permutation of its incident edge indices from most to least preferred. Vertex and edge indices are binary encoded with ordinary length-delimited list syntax; the input length \(L\) counts every listed vertex, incidence and preference entry. The incidence matrix is \(A_{v,j}=1\) for \(v\in e_j\) and zero otherwise. The promise is total unimodularity: every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). A matching \(M\subseteq E\) consists of pairwise disjoint edges. Every vertex prefers any incident edge to remaining unmatched. An edge \(e\notin M\) blocks \(M\) if every \(v\in e\) is unmatched or strictly prefers \(e\) to the unique edge of \(M\) containing \(v\). Stability means no edge blocks. There are no ties, capacities above one, edge-size bounds or optimization objective. Use one deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, randomness or an oracle, running within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) on every input string. It must return a list of edge indices forming a stable matching on every well-formed promised instance; its answer outside that promise is unrestricted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a uniform polynomial-time algorithm satisfying the stated search specification on all promised instances, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A conditional complexity lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. Fractional existence, finding a stable solution in a proper subclass, and optimizing the weight of a stable solution are distinct targets.

context_blocks.title: Coalitions rather than pairs
context_blocks.text: A hyperedge represents a group that could cooperate. Selected groups cannot share members. Stability forbids an unselected group whose members would all prefer forming it to their current situation. The input includes each participant’s ranking, so merely finding disjoint groups is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: Existence and computation
context_blocks.text: The source explains why total unimodularity together with a classical stable-fractional existence theorem guarantees an integral stable matching. It does not give a general polynomial running-time bound. Hardness of maximizing weight among stable matchings is a different question from finding any stable one.

context_blocks.title: A newer special-case result
context_blocks.text: An August 2026 preprint gives a polynomial-time algorithm for network hypergraphs. In that class the ground elements are arcs of an oriented tree and each hyperedge is a directed tree path. Network hypergraphs are a subclass of unimodular hypergraphs, so this narrows the open frontier without resolving the general target.

Without a structural promise, stability can fail even for groups of size two. On three vertices with possible pairs ab, bc and ca, let a prefer ab to ca, b prefer bc to ab, and c prefer ca to bc. Every chosen pair is blocked by another pair, and the empty matching is blocked as well. The incidence matrix of this triangle has a square determinant of magnitude two, so it is outside the totally unimodular domain.

The objective is to return any stable matching. Different vertices may favor different stable outcomes, but the card imposes no social-welfare, maximum-cardinality, or weighted objective. This distinction matters because optimizing over stable outcomes can be hard even in a class where finding one outcome is efficient.

cards.context:
A hyperedge represents a group that could cooperate. Selected groups cannot share members. Stability forbids an unselected group whose members would all prefer forming it to their current situation. The input includes each participant’s ranking, so merely finding disjoint groups is insufficient.

The source explains why total unimodularity together with a classical stable-fractional existence theorem guarantees an integral stable matching. It does not give a general polynomial running-time bound. Hardness of maximizing weight among stable matchings is a different question from finding any stable one.

An August 2026 preprint gives a polynomial-time algorithm for network hypergraphs. In that class the ground elements are arcs of an oriented tree and each hyperedge is a directed tree path. Network hypergraphs are a subclass of unimodular hypergraphs, so this narrows the open frontier without resolving the general target.

Without a structural promise, stability can fail even for groups of size two. On three vertices with possible pairs ab, bc and ca, let a prefer ab to ca, b prefer bc to ab, and c prefer ca to bc. Every chosen pair is blocked by another pair, and the empty matching is blocked as well. The incidence matrix of this triangle has a square determinant of magnitude two, so it is outside the totally unimodular domain.

The objective is to return any stable matching. Different vertices may favor different stable outcomes, but the card imposes no social-welfare, maximum-cardinality, or weighted objective. This distinction matters because optimizing over stable outcomes can be hard even in a class where finding one outcome is efficient.

cards.definitions:
A game has a finite nonempty state set \(S\), a specified initial state \(s_0\), and two players \(i\in\{1,2\}\). At each state \(s\), player \(i\) has a finite nonempty action set \(A_i(s)\). Both players choose actions simultaneously. A deterministic transition function maps \((s,a_1,a_2)\) to the next state. There is no additional random transition mechanism.

Terminal states are absorbing: every legal action pair leaves their state unchanged. Each terminal state \(f\) has a fixed finite real reward \(r_i(f)\geq0\) for each player. A play that first reaches \(f\) gives player \(i\) the one-time payoff \(r_i(f)\). A play that never reaches a terminal state gives zero. There are no intermediate rewards, discounting or repeated payments after absorption. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed.

A strategy \(\sigma_i\) assigns a probability distribution on \(A_i(s_t)\) to every finite visited-state history \(s_0s_1\cdots s_t\). At each round, actions are drawn independently for the two players according to these distributions. The strategy has access to state history, not the history of either player's chosen actions. This is the source's action-insensitive behavioral model, called “mixed strategies” there. It permits arbitrary history dependence and real probabilities; neither finite memory nor computability is required.

The transition rule and strategies induce a probability distribution on infinite plays. Let \(u_i(\sigma_1,\sigma_2;s_0)\) be the expected one-time payoff, including zero on nontermination. Rewards are bounded because the game is finite, so this expectation is well defined. A profile is an exact Nash equilibrium from \(s_0\) if
\[
u_i(\tau_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)\leq u_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)
\]
for both players and every alternative strategy \(\tau_i\) in the same state-history model. The other player's strategy stays fixed.

The question quantifies over every such finite game and initial state. It asks for an equilibrium against all permitted deviations, not merely stationary deviations, and does not require an equilibrium after every possible history as subgame perfection would. No payoff threshold, welfare guarantee or algorithm for constructing the profile is part of the target. Positive scaling of a player's rewards preserves the question, but adding a constant only at terminals need not: infinite plays still receive zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that an exact equilibrium exists for every game and initial state in the specified two-player, nonnegative, state-history model, or give a finite game in that model and prove that no permitted strategy profile is an exact equilibrium from its initial state. A failure of stationary or finite-memory equilibria alone is insufficient. Approximate equilibria and equilibria under imprecise deviations do not meet the exact criterion.
